entities.name: Global
entities.summary: Cross-regional and worldwide frames (BCE/CE, prehistoric ages, world wars).

entities.name: Europe
entities.summary: From the Aegean Bronze Age through the modern EU. Split into Mediterranean, Western, Central, Northern, and Eastern sub-branches.

entities.name: West Asia
entities.summary: Mesopotamia, the Levant, Anatolia, Iran, and Arabia.

entities.name: Central Asia & the Steppe
entities.summary: Silk Road oases, the Eurasian steppe, and Tibet.

entities.name: South Asia
entities.summary: Indian subcontinent from Indus civilization through the modern republics.

entities.name: Cross-Regional Empires
entities.summary: Empires spanning multiple regions — cross-linked here for convenience.

entities.name: BCE (Before Common Era)
entities.summary: The 'before Common Era' convention for years prior to year 1. Equivalent to BC.

entities.name: CE (Common Era)
entities.summary: The 'Common Era' convention for years from year 1 onward. Equivalent to AD.

entities.name: Paleolithic (Old Stone Age)
entities.summary: The long first chapter: stone tools, fire, and hunter-gatherer life, from the earliest knapped stone through the whole span of the genus Homo.
entities.date_note: Starts at the earliest known stone tools — Lomekwi 3, c. 3.3 Ma — which predate the genus Homo. Whether those count as Oldowan is a definitional argument; they are included here because the toolmaking record is continuous even where the taxonomy is not.

entities.name: Mesolithic
entities.date_note: A Eurasian term. It has no counterpart in the Americas, sub-Saharan Africa or Australia, where the post-glacial sequence is described differently.

entities.name: Neolithic (New Stone Age)
entities.summary: Beginnings of agriculture, animal domestication, and permanent villages.

entities.name: Bronze Age
entities.date_note: Regional Bronze Ages began at different dates; the collapse cluster is c. 1200-1150 BCE.
entities.summary: Age of bronze metallurgy, ending in the systemic Late Bronze Age Collapse c. 1200 BCE.

entities.name: Iron Age
entities.summary: Widespread adoption of iron for weapons and tools; the age of classical antiquity's origins.

entities.name: Classical Antiquity
entities.summary: The Greek and Roman world, roughly from Homer to the fall of Western Rome.

entities.name: Middle Ages
entities.summary: Between the fall of Rome and the Renaissance; medieval Christendom, the Islamic Golden Age, Tang-Song China, and Kamakura Japan.

entities.name: Early Modern
entities.summary: Age of exploration, colonial empires, and gunpowder; from ~1500 to the eve of the Napoleonic Wars.

entities.name: Long 19th Century
entities.summary: Historians' 'long nineteenth century' from the French Revolution to World War I.

entities.name: Short 20th Century
entities.summary: Hobsbawm's 'short twentieth century' from WWI to the collapse of the Soviet Union.

entities.name: Contemporary
entities.summary: Post-Cold-War world: globalization, digital revolution, climate crisis.

entities.name: Ancient Egypt
entities.summary: Continuous Nile Valley civilization from Predynastic cultures through Narmer's unification, the pharaonic dynasties, and Ptolemaic/Roman/Byzantine rule.

entities.name: Early Dynastic Period
entities.summary: Unification of Upper and Lower Egypt under the 1st and 2nd Dynasties.

entities.name: Narmer / Menes
entities.summary: Legendary unifier of Upper and Lower Egypt. Dates and identity as Menes are partly traditional.

entities.name: Old Kingdom
entities.summary: Pyramid-building age. Djoser, Khufu, Khafre, Menkaure.

entities.name: Djoser
entities.summary: Commissioned the Step Pyramid at Saqqara, the world's first monumental stone building.

entities.name: Khufu
entities.summary: Builder of the Great Pyramid of Giza.

entities.name: Khafre
entities.summary: Built the second Giza pyramid and, by tradition, the Great Sphinx.

entities.name: Pepi II
entities.summary: Traditionally credited with the longest reign in history (~94 years).

entities.name: First Intermediate Period
entities.summary: Political fragmentation between the Old and Middle Kingdoms.

entities.name: Middle Kingdom
entities.summary: Second great age of pharaonic Egypt after reunification under Mentuhotep II; classical Egyptian literature.

entities.name: 11th Dynasty (reunified)
entities.date_note: Early 11th Dynasty (Theban Intefs) predates the reunification that starts the Middle Kingdom.

entities.name: Mentuhotep II
entities.summary: Reunified Egypt, founding the Middle Kingdom.

entities.name: Second Intermediate Period
entities.summary: Hyksos rule in the Delta; Theban resistance in the south.

entities.name: 15th Dynasty — Hyksos
entities.summary: Semitic-speaking rulers who introduced the horse and chariot, composite bow, and bronze weapons.

entities.name: New Kingdom
entities.summary: Imperial age of Egypt; Valley of the Kings; Karnak/Luxor expansion.

entities.name: Ahmose I
entities.summary: Expelled the Hyksos and founded the New Kingdom.

entities.name: Hatshepsut
entities.summary: Female pharaoh who ruled as king in her own right; built the Deir el-Bahri temple.

entities.name: Thutmose III
entities.summary: Great warrior-pharaoh; extended the empire to its widest historical extent.

entities.name: Akhenaten
entities.summary: Founded a short-lived monotheistic cult of the Aten and moved the capital to Amarna.

entities.name: Tutankhamun
entities.summary: Reversed the Amarna religious reforms. His intact tomb was discovered in 1922.

entities.name: Ramesses II
entities.summary: Long-reigning warrior-pharaoh. Fought the Hittites at Kadesh and signed the world's earliest surviving peace treaty.

entities.name: Ramesses III
entities.summary: Last great New Kingdom pharaoh; repelled the Sea Peoples.

entities.name: 25th Dynasty — Kushite (Nubian)
entities.summary: Nubian pharaohs from Kush ruled all Egypt.

entities.name: Ptolemaic Egypt
entities.summary: Greek-Macedonian dynasty founded after Alexander's conquest. Capital: Alexandria.

entities.name: Cleopatra VII
entities.summary: Last active pharaoh of Egypt. Allied with Julius Caesar and Mark Antony; defeated at Actium in 31 BCE.

entities.name: Kingdom of Kush
entities.summary: Nubian civilization south of Egypt with capitals successively at Kerma, Napata, and Meroë.

entities.name: Meroitic Phase
entities.summary: Meroë as capital; Meroitic script still undeciphered.

entities.name: Kingdom of Aksum
entities.summary: Highland Ethiopian empire; converted to Christianity under Ezana (c. 330 CE).

entities.name: Ezana
entities.summary: Made Aksum one of the earliest Christian states.

entities.name: Ethiopian Empire
entities.summary: Solomonic dynasty ruled Ethiopia for seven centuries; never fully colonized.

entities.name: Menelik II
entities.summary: Defeated Italy at the Battle of Adwa (1896).

entities.name: Haile Selassie
entities.summary: Long-reigning modernizing Ethiopian emperor; deposed in the 1974 revolution.

entities.name: Jōmon Period
entities.summary: Hunter-gatherer culture famous for cord-marked pottery.

entities.name: Kofun Period
entities.summary: Age of keyhole-shaped tumulus tombs.

entities.name: Heian Period
entities.summary: Classical age of Japanese court culture; The Tale of Genji.

entities.name: Kamakura Period
entities.summary: First shogunate; repelled two Mongol invasions.

entities.name: Muromachi / Nanboku-chō Period
entities.summary: Ashikaga shōgunate; culturally rich but politically fragmenting into the Sengoku warring-states era.

entities.name: Azuchi–Momoyama Period
entities.summary: Unification wars under Oda Nobunaga, Toyotomi Hideyoshi, and Tokugawa Ieyasu.

entities.name: Oda Nobunaga
entities.date_note: Oda Nobunaga's rule began 1568, before the formal Azuchi-Momoyama era start (1573).
entities.summary: Ruthless unifier who broke the political power of Buddhist monasteries and rival warlords.

entities.name: Toyotomi Hideyoshi
entities.summary: Peasant-born unifier who completed Nobunaga's project and invaded Korea (Imjin War).

entities.name: Edo Period
entities.summary: Tokugawa shogunate; long peace, sakoku isolation, cultural flowering.

entities.name: Tokugawa Ieyasu
entities.summary: Founder of the Tokugawa shogunate.

entities.name: Modern Japan
entities.summary: From the Meiji Restoration to the present. One nengō per emperor.

entities.name: Meiji
entities.summary: Meiji Restoration and rapid modernization. Emperor Meiji (Mutsuhito).

entities.name: Taishō
entities.summary: Democratic reform era; Emperor Taishō (Yoshihito).

entities.name: Shōwa
entities.summary: Longest modern era. Emperor Shōwa (Hirohito). Spans militarism, WWII, and postwar boom.

entities.name: Heisei
entities.summary: Emperor Akihito. Ended by voluntary abdication.

entities.name: Reiwa
entities.summary: Current era. Emperor Naruhito.

entities.name: Wadō
entities.date_note: Nengō began 708 in Asuka, continued into Nara (710).

entities.name: Enryaku
entities.date_note: Nengō 782-806 spans the Nara-Heian boundary (794).

entities.name: Genkō (元弘)
entities.date_note: Nengō 1331-1334 spans the Kamakura-Kenmu boundary (1333).

entities.name: Engen
entities.summary: Southern Court nengō during the Nanboku-chō schism.

entities.name: Kōkoku
entities.summary: Southern Court nengō during the Nanboku-chō schism.

entities.summary: Southern Court nengō during the Nanboku-chō schism.

entities.date_note: Northern-Court nengō predating the formal Muromachi start (1336).

entities.summary: Northern Court nengō during the Nanboku-chō schism.

entities.summary: Northern Court nengō during the Nanboku-chō schism.

entities.summary: Northern Court nengō during the Nanboku-chō schism.

entities.summary: Northern Court nengō during the Nanboku-chō schism.

entities.summary: Northern Court nengō during the Nanboku-chō schism.

entities.name: Jōji
entities.summary: Northern Court nengō during the Nanboku-chō schism.

entities.name: Ōan
entities.summary: Northern Court nengō during the Nanboku-chō schism.

entities.name: Eiwa
entities.summary: Northern Court nengō during the Nanboku-chō schism.

entities.name: Kōryaku
entities.summary: Northern Court nengō during the Nanboku-chō schism.

entities.name: Eitoku
entities.summary: Northern Court nengō during the Nanboku-chō schism.

entities.name: Shitoku
entities.summary: Northern Court nengō during the Nanboku-chō schism.

entities.name: Kakei
entities.summary: Northern Court nengō during the Nanboku-chō schism.

entities.name: Kōō
entities.summary: Northern Court nengō during the Nanboku-chō schism.

entities.name: Meitoku
entities.summary: Northern Court nengō during the Nanboku-chō schism.

entities.name: Keichō
entities.date_note: Nengō 1596-1615 spans Azuchi-Momoyama into early Edo.

entities.name: Shang Dynasty
entities.summary: First historically confirmed Chinese dynasty. Oracle bones; bronze ritual vessels.

entities.name: Zhou Dynasty
entities.summary: Longest dynasty in Chinese history. Split into Western and Eastern (Spring-Autumn + Warring States).

entities.name: Spring and Autumn Period
entities.summary: Time of Confucius and Laozi.

entities.name: Warring States Period
entities.summary: Seven kingdoms fought for supremacy; Hundred Schools of Thought.
entities.date_note: Warring States is a historiographic period that outlasted the nominal Eastern Zhou.

entities.name: Qin Dynasty
entities.summary: First unified imperial state.

entities.name: Qin Shi Huangdi
entities.summary: First Emperor of unified China. Standardized script, currency, and weights. Terracotta Army.

entities.name: Han Dynasty
entities.summary: Classical Chinese empire; namesake of the Han Chinese ethnicity.

entities.name: Emperor Wu
entities.summary: Made Confucianism the state ideology; opened the Silk Road via Zhang Qian.

entities.name: Eastern Han
entities.summary: Paper invented by Cai Lun (c. 105); Buddhism enters China.

entities.name: Three Kingdoms
entities.summary: Wei, Shu, and Wu — the era of the Romance of the Three Kingdoms.

entities.name: Tang Dynasty
entities.summary: Golden age of Chinese poetry and cosmopolitan trade.

entities.name: Empress Wu Zetian
entities.summary: Only woman to rule China as emperor in her own right.

entities.name: Song Dynasty
entities.summary: Economic and technological golden age: printing, gunpowder, compass, paper money.

entities.name: Yuan Dynasty
entities.date_note: Yuan formally ended in 1368 when the Ming took Beijing; Huizong ruled from Mongolia until 1370 (Northern Yuan).
entities.summary: Mongol-ruled China under the descendants of Genghis Khan.

links.note: Mongol-ruled dynasty in China after the fragmentation of the unified empire.
Overthrown by the Ming, which claimed the Mandate of Heaven.

entities.name: Kublai Khan
entities.summary: Grandson of Genghis; founder of the Yuan Dynasty.
entities.date_note: Kublai was Great Khan from 1260; founded the Yuan dynasty in 1271.

entities.name: Ming Dynasty
entities.summary: Restored Han Chinese rule; Zheng He's voyages; Forbidden City built.

entities.name: Yongle Emperor
entities.summary: Commissioned Zheng He's treasure voyages; moved capital to Beijing.

entities.name: Qing Dynasty
entities.summary: Manchu-ruled last imperial dynasty.

entities.name: Kangxi Emperor
entities.summary: Longest-reigning Qing emperor; consolidated Manchu rule and expanded the empire.

entities.name: Qianlong Emperor
entities.summary: Cultural peak of the Qing; long reign ending in stagnation.

entities.name: Republic of China
entities.summary: Post-imperial China, ending on the mainland with the Communist victory in 1949; continues on Taiwan.

entities.name: People's Republic of China
entities.summary: Founded by Mao Zedong in 1949; the world's most populous state until 2023.

entities.name: Three Kingdoms of Korea
entities.summary: Goguryeo, Baekje, Silla.

entities.name: Goryeo Dynasty
entities.summary: Origin of the name 'Korea'; celadon ceramics; movable metal type.

entities.name: Joseon Dynasty
entities.summary: Long-lived Confucian monarchy; Hangul script created under Sejong the Great.

entities.name: King Sejong the Great
entities.summary: Fourth Joseon king; commissioned the Hangul script.

entities.name: Japanese Colonial Rule
entities.summary: Japanese annexation of Korea (1910–1945); ended by WWII.

entities.name: Divided Korea
entities.summary: Postwar division into North and South Korea after the Korean War.

entities.name: Sumerian Early Dynastic
entities.summary: World's first cities: Uruk, Ur, Lagash, Kish.

entities.name: Gilgamesh (legendary)
entities.summary: Legendary king of Uruk; hero of the eponymous epic.

entities.name: Akkadian Empire
entities.summary: First empire in world history.

entities.name: Sargon of Akkad
entities.summary: Founder of the Akkadian Empire; considered the first empire-builder in world history.

entities.name: Old Babylonian Empire
entities.summary: Amorite dynasty of Babylon; Hammurabi's law code.

entities.name: Hammurabi
entities.summary: Famous for the Code of Hammurabi, one of the earliest surviving law codes.

entities.name: Assyrian Empires
entities.summary: Ancient Mesopotamian empires that dominated the Near East in the Iron Age.

entities.name: Neo-Assyrian Empire
entities.summary: Mass deportations as imperial policy; library of Nineveh.

entities.name: Neo-Babylonian Empire
entities.summary: Chaldean dynasty that overthrew Assyria; Nebuchadnezzar destroyed Jerusalem in 587 BCE.

entities.name: Nebuchadnezzar II
entities.summary: Destroyed Jerusalem (587 BCE); traditional builder of the Hanging Gardens.

entities.name: Kingdoms of Israel and Judah
entities.summary: Iron Age Hebrew kingdoms.

entities.name: David
entities.summary: Traditional second king of Israel; united the northern and southern kingdoms.

entities.name: Solomon
entities.summary: Traditional builder of the First Temple in Jerusalem.

entities.name: Phoenician City-States
entities.summary: Tyre, Sidon, Byblos. Founded Carthage and colonized the Mediterranean.

entities.name: Achaemenid Empire
entities.summary: First Persian empire; largest of its time.

entities.name: Cyrus II the Great
entities.summary: Founder of the Achaemenid Empire; freed the Jews from Babylonian exile.
entities.date_note: Cyrus II ruled Persia from 559, becoming founder of the Achaemenid empire in 550.

entities.name: Cambyses II
entities.summary: Conquered Egypt (525 BCE).

entities.name: Darius I the Great
entities.summary: Great organizer; built Persepolis; invaded Greece and lost at Marathon.

entities.name: Xerxes I
entities.summary: Led the second Persian invasion of Greece; lost at Salamis and Plataea.

entities.name: Darius III
entities.summary: Last Achaemenid; defeated by Alexander the Great.

entities.name: Seleucid Empire
entities.summary: Hellenistic successor state to Alexander's eastern conquests; the biggest single Diadochi kingdom.

entities.name: Parthian (Arsacid) Empire
entities.summary: Iranian empire that ruled Persia and Mesopotamia for four centuries; Rome's chief eastern rival.

entities.name: Sasanian Empire
entities.summary: Last pre-Islamic Persian empire; peer superpower of Rome/Byzantium.

entities.name: Shapur I
entities.summary: Captured Roman Emperor Valerian alive at Edessa (260 CE).

entities.name: Khosrow I Anushirvan
entities.summary: Golden-age king; legal and administrative reforms.

entities.name: Safavid Empire
entities.summary: Made Shia Islam the state religion.

entities.name: Pahlavi Dynasty
entities.summary: Last royal dynasty of Iran; overthrown by the 1979 Islamic Revolution.

entities.name: Islamic Republic of Iran
entities.summary: Theocratic state established by Ayatollah Khomeini after the 1979 revolution.

entities.name: Rise of Islam
entities.summary: Muhammad's prophetic career and the birth of Islam.

entities.name: Prophet Muhammad
entities.summary: Founder of Islam; united most of Arabia under his rule by 632.

entities.name: Rashidun Caliphate
entities.summary: First four 'rightly guided' caliphs; rapid conquest of Persia, Levant, and Egypt.

entities.name: Umayyad Caliphate
entities.summary: Dynasty ruling from Damascus. Reached from Iberia to Central Asia.

entities.name: Abbasid Caliphate
entities.summary: Ruled from Baghdad; Islamic Golden Age. Ended by Mongol sack of Baghdad.

entities.name: Harun al-Rashid
entities.summary: Fifth Abbasid caliph; his court is the setting of many One Thousand and One Nights tales.

entities.name: Fatimid Caliphate
entities.summary: Isma'ili Shia caliphate; founded Cairo and Al-Azhar.

entities.name: Ottoman Empire
entities.summary: Multi-continental empire spanning Anatolia, the Balkans, North Africa, and the Arab world.

entities.name: Mehmed II the Conqueror
entities.summary: Conquered Constantinople in 1453, ending the Byzantine Empire.

entities.name: Suleiman I the Magnificent
entities.summary: Longest-reigning Ottoman sultan; peak of Ottoman power and cultural achievement.

entities.name: Ancient Greece
entities.summary: Cradle of Western philosophy, drama, historiography, and democracy.

entities.name: Minoan Civilization
entities.summary: Bronze Age Cretan civilization; palace at Knossos.

entities.name: Mycenaean Civilization
entities.summary: Late Bronze Age Greek civilization; the world of Homer's epics.

entities.name: Archaic Greece
entities.summary: Formative period of the polis, colonization, and archaic art.

entities.name: Classical Greece
entities.summary: Age of Athens' Golden Age, the Peloponnesian War, and philosophers Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle.

entities.name: Pericles (statesman)
entities.summary: Athenian statesman who led the city through its cultural Golden Age.

entities.name: Kingdom of Macedon
entities.summary: Northern Greek kingdom that under Philip II and Alexander conquered the classical world.

entities.name: Philip II of Macedon
entities.summary: Reorganized the Macedonian army and unified Greece under Macedonian hegemony.

entities.name: Alexander the Great
entities.summary: Conquered the Achaemenid Empire, reaching India. Ushered in the Hellenistic Age.

entities.name: Hellenistic Period
entities.summary: Age of Greek-influenced kingdoms from Alexander's death to Actium.

entities.name: Ancient Rome
entities.summary: From the legendary founding to the fall of the Western Empire; the political and cultural core of the ancient Mediterranean.

entities.name: Roman Kingdom
entities.summary: Seven legendary kings from Romulus to Tarquin the Proud.

entities.name: Roman Republic
entities.summary: Non-monarchical Rome governed by the Senate and elected magistrates.

entities.name: Late Republic
entities.summary: Era of Marius, Sulla, Pompey, Caesar, and Octavian; ended by civil wars that produced the Empire.

entities.name: Julius Caesar
entities.summary: Dictator perpetuo; assassinated on the Ides of March, 44 BCE.

entities.name: Roman Empire
entities.summary: Monarchical Roman state from Augustus's Principate to the deposition of Romulus Augustulus.

entities.name: Augustus
entities.summary: First Roman emperor; founder of the Principate.

entities.name: Nero
entities.summary: Fifth Roman emperor; committed suicide after being declared a public enemy.

entities.name: Nerva–Antonine Dynasty
entities.summary: Five Good Emperors; Pax Romana at its peak.

entities.name: Trajan
entities.summary: Extended Rome to its greatest territorial extent.

entities.name: Hadrian
entities.summary: Consolidator emperor who built Hadrian's Wall in Britain.

entities.name: Marcus Aurelius
entities.summary: Philosopher-emperor and author of the Meditations.

entities.name: Constantine the Great
entities.summary: Legalized Christianity; founded Constantinople.

entities.name: Byzantine Empire
entities.summary: Roman Empire's Greek-speaking continuation, based in Constantinople.

entities.name: Justinian I
entities.summary: Reconquered much of the western Mediterranean; codified Roman law; built Hagia Sophia.

entities.name: Constantine XI Palaiologos
entities.summary: Last Byzantine emperor; killed defending Constantinople.

entities.name: Carolingian Empire
entities.summary: Frankish empire founded by Charlemagne; briefly reunified western Europe.

entities.name: Charlemagne
entities.summary: First Emperor of the Romans since antiquity; crowned by Pope Leo III in 800.

entities.name: France (Medieval to Modern)
entities.summary: Kingdom (later republic) of France from Hugh Capet to the present.

entities.name: Bourbon France
entities.summary: Longest-ruling French royal house; ended by the French Revolution.

entities.name: Louis XIV (Sun King)
entities.summary: Longest reign of any European monarch; built Versailles.

entities.name: French Revolution
entities.summary: Overthrew the Bourbon monarchy and reshaped modern politics.

entities.name: Napoleonic Era
entities.summary: Napoleon Bonaparte's dominance of Europe from consul to emperor and exile.

entities.name: Napoleon I
entities.summary: Emperor of the French; conquered most of continental Europe before defeat at Waterloo (1815).

entities.name: England (Medieval to Modern)
entities.summary: Kingdom of England (later Great Britain, then United Kingdom).

entities.name: Norman England
entities.summary: Norman-French dynasty founded by William the Conqueror.

entities.name: William the Conqueror
entities.summary: Conquered England at Hastings (1066).

entities.name: Tudor England
entities.summary: House that ruled England 1485–1603 including Henry VIII and Elizabeth I.

entities.name: Henry VIII
entities.summary: Broke with Rome to form the Church of England; had six wives.

entities.name: Elizabeth I
entities.summary: Presided over England's Elizabethan Golden Age of drama and exploration.

entities.name: Victorian Britain
entities.summary: Long reign of Queen Victoria; peak of the British Empire.

entities.name: Queen Victoria
entities.summary: Symbol of the age that bears her name; her descendants sit on many European thrones.

entities.name: Spanish Empire
entities.summary: First truly global empire; the leading colonial power of the 16th century.

entities.name: Portuguese Empire
entities.summary: Pioneered European maritime exploration; earliest and longest-lived colonial empire.

entities.name: Holy Roman Empire
entities.summary: Multi-ethnic complex of European territories notionally under an elected emperor.

entities.name: Habsburg Era
entities.summary: Habsburg dynasty held the Holy Roman Emperor title almost continuously from 1438 to 1806.

entities.name: Charles V
entities.summary: Ruled an empire on which the sun never set: Spain, the HRE, Naples, the Netherlands, and Spanish America.

entities.name: German Empire
entities.summary: Unified German state 1871–1918 under the Hohenzollerns; collapsed at the end of WWI.

entities.name: Nazi Germany
entities.summary: Totalitarian state under Hitler; started WWII in Europe and perpetrated the Holocaust.

entities.name: Post-War Germany
entities.summary: Federal Republic of Germany from 1949 (reunified 1990).

entities.name: Viking Age
entities.summary: Norse expansion across northern Europe and the North Atlantic.

entities.name: Kievan Rus'
entities.summary: Medieval East Slavic federation; ancestor state of modern Russia, Ukraine, and Belarus.

entities.name: Tsardom of Russia
entities.summary: Russian state from Ivan IV's assumption of the tsar title to Peter I's imperial declaration.

entities.name: Ivan IV the Terrible
entities.summary: Ivan the Terrible; expanded Russia and established the Oprichnina reign of terror.

entities.name: Russian Empire
entities.summary: Multi-national empire from Peter the Great to the abdication of Nicholas II.

entities.name: Peter the Great
entities.date_note: Peter I reigned as tsar from 1682; declared himself emperor in 1721, founding the Russian Empire.
entities.summary: Westernizing tsar who founded St. Petersburg and made Russia a major European power.

entities.name: Catherine the Great
entities.summary: German-born empress who expanded Russia to the Black Sea and patronized the arts.

entities.name: Soviet Union
entities.summary: Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (USSR); communist superpower 1922–1991.

entities.name: Vladimir Lenin
entities.date_note: Lenin led the Russian SFSR from 1917; the USSR was formally created in 1922.
entities.summary: Bolshevik leader; founded the Soviet state after the October Revolution.

entities.name: Joseph Stalin
entities.summary: Longtime dictator; industrialized the USSR at enormous human cost and led it through WWII.

entities.name: Russian Federation
entities.summary: Russian Federation from 1991 to the present.

entities.name: Xiongnu Empire
entities.summary: First great nomadic empire on the Mongolian plateau.

entities.name: Kushan Empire
entities.summary: Yuezhi-descended empire linking China, India, and Rome via the Silk Road.

entities.name: Mongol Empire
entities.summary: Largest contiguous empire in world history.

entities.summary: Genghis Khan; founder of the largest contiguous land empire in world history.

entities.name: Human Prehistory
entities.summary: From the earliest stone toolmaking to the first written records. Dated by measurement rather than reckoning, so quoted in years before present.
entities.date_note: SCOPE GATE. This app begins where human-like BEHAVIOUR begins, not where a taxon does. The floor is the earliest knapped stone — currently Lomekwi 3 at 3.3 Ma, which predates the oldest Homo fossil by about 500,000 years. A taxonomic floor would exclude the oldest instance of the very behaviour this app exists to track, and taxonomy is the least stable line available: H. habilis placement is disputed and the Ledi-Geraru mandible is unnamed. Knapping is the line rather than tool use, because tool use extends to chimpanzees and orangutans and so runs past the ~7 Ma common ancestor, which would make any floor arbitrary. The end is diachronous: writing appears at different times in different regions.

caveats.text: The floor is a behaviour, not a site. If an older knapping site is accepted, this date moves and the app's scope does not change.

entities.name: Hominins
entities.summary: Humans, proto-humans and near-humans: a dozen or so named species, most of which overlapped with others rather than succeeding them in a line.
entities.date_note: The earliest fossil attributed to Homo is LD 350-1 from Ledi-Geraru, Ethiopia, at 2.80-2.75 Ma, constrained by the Gurumaha Tuff at 2.782 +/- 0.006 Ma. The genus is ongoing, so it outlasts prehistory rather than ending with it.

alternatives.label: LD 350-1 not assignable to Homo
alternatives.note: Argues the mandible cannot be unequivocally attributed to Homo, which would leave the genus with no securely dated fossil this early.

entities.name: Homo habilis
entities.date_note: Whether the material forms one species, and whether it belongs in Homo at all, is still argued. The late specimen KNM-ER 42703 is 1.44 Ma.

caveats.text: Some researchers would move this material out of Homo entirely, which would change where our genus begins.

entities.summary: An early, small-brained human in Africa from about 2.4 to 1.4 million years ago, overlapping with other human species.

entities.name: Homo rudolfensis
entities.date_note: Type specimen KNM-ER 1470, Koobi Fora. Four hominin species coexisted in the Turkana Basin between 2.0 and 1.5 Ma.

caveats.text: Some researchers assign this material to Homo habilis rather than to a separate species.

entities.summary: A flat-faced, big-toothed early human from Kenya about 1.9 million years ago whose place in the human genus is still argued over.

entities.name: Homo erectus
entities.date_note: Treated here sensu lato, including African material sometimes separated as H. ergaster. The terminal Ngandong date rests on Bayesian modelling of 52 radiometric estimates.
entities.summary: The first widely travelled human species, present from about 1.9 million years ago until roughly 110,000 years ago in Java.

entities.name: Homo antecessor
entities.date_note: Gran Dolina level TD6 dates to 780-857 ka. The young limit is fixed by reversed Matuyama polarity, which requires an age greater than 780 ka.
entities.summary: An early European human from a Spanish cave, about 800,000 years old, whose status as a separate species is still argued.

entities.name: Homo heidelbergensis
entities.date_note: Range may reach 1.3 Ma if older Spanish and Italian material is included.

caveats.text: Functions partly as a catch-all for Middle Pleistocene humans; several proposed splits would dismantle it.

entities.summary: A large-brained Middle Pleistocene human in Europe, Africa and the Near East, roughly 700,000 to 200,000 years ago.

entities.name: Homo naledi
entities.date_note: Its position in the human family tree is unresolved.
entities.summary: A small-brained human found deep in a South African cave system, surprisingly recent at 335,000 to 236,000 years ago.

entities.name: Homo neanderthalensis
entities.date_note: The extinction date is not uniform across the range; the associated Mousterian ends 41,030-39,260 cal BP.
entities.summary: Cold-adapted humans across Europe and western Asia, from about 400,000 years ago until roughly 40,000 years ago.

entities.name: Denisovans
entities.date_note: Genetically unambiguous but with no formally accepted species name and no type specimen in the conventional sense.
entities.summary: A human population known mainly from DNA, identified from fragments in a Siberian cave and traceable in living people.

entities.name: Homo floresiensis
entities.date_note: Skeletal remains to about 60 ka, associated artefacts from about 190 ka and continuing to about 50 ka.

alternatives.label: Original 2004 chronology
alternatives.note: Withdrawn in 2016: the dated deposits proved to be a younger unit unconformably overlying the remains.

caveats.text: Often reported as surviving until 12,000 years ago. That date was corrected to around 60,000 in 2016.

entities.summary: A small-bodied human on the Indonesian island of Flores, known from Liang Bua cave.

entities.name: Homo luzonensis
entities.date_note: Minimum age revised upward to at least 134 ka in 2023. No youngest-remains date is established; the original 67 ka metatarsal age is now read as a minimum from the dating method rather than a true age.
entities.summary: A human species known from a handful of bones and teeth in a cave on Luzon, the Philippines.

entities.name: Homo sapiens
entities.date_note: 315 +/- 34 ka is the thermoluminescence age of heated flints with the Jebel Irhoud hominins in Morocco. Which fossils count as H. sapiens is itself part of the disagreement about the date.
entities.summary: Our own species, first recognisable in Africa around 300,000 years ago.

entities.name: Homo longi
entities.date_note: Known from one cranium with a minimum U-series age of about 146 ka, so there is no species-level range.

alternatives.label: Harbin cranium is Denisovan
alternatives.note: Palaeoproteomic analysis in 2025 recovered 95 endogenous proteins and clustered the specimen with Denisova 3.

caveats.text: Named as a new species in 2021; 2025 protein evidence indicates the specimen is a Denisovan.

entities.summary: A single large skull from Harbin, China, whose identity was overturned by protein analysis in 2025.

entities.name: Oldowan Industry
entities.date_note: Usually given as 2.6-1.7 Ma. Older claims exist, but the 3.3 Ma Lomekwi 3 tools are excluded by classifying them as Lomekwian, so the boundary is definitional as much as evidential.
entities.summary: The earliest widely recognised stone tools: sharp flakes struck from pebble cores.

entities.name: Acheulean Industry
entities.date_note: Earliest at Kokiselei 4, West Turkana, Kenya, at 1.76 Ma — about 350,000 years earlier than previously accepted. The end is diffuse rather than dated.
entities.summary: The handaxe tradition: teardrop-shaped tools worked on both faces, made for well over a million years.

entities.name: Mousterian Industry
entities.date_note: Hard to separate from the latest Acheulean at the start, so the beginning is definitional. The end differs by region and by method.
entities.summary: The flake-tool tradition associated mainly with Neanderthals across Europe and western Asia.

entities.name: Aterian Industry
entities.date_note: 145 +/- 9 ka is the weighted-mean thermoluminescence age at El Mnasra. The industry is defined by tool shape rather than by date, so its limits move with the definition.
entities.summary: A North African tradition marked by tanged points, made by early modern humans across the Sahara.

entities.name: Still Bay Industry
entities.date_note: Single-grain OSL makes this a short episode of under 5,000 years.

alternatives.label: Diepkloof thermoluminescence chronology
alternatives.note: TL at Diepkloof puts the Still Bay some 35,000 years earlier than the single-grain OSL chronology.

entities.summary: A brief South African tradition of finely worked leaf-shaped points, an early flowering of complex technique.

entities.name: Howiesons Poort Industry
entities.date_note: Single-grain OSL makes this a tight horizon marker; ESR and TL at Klasies River give a looser 50,000-60,000 years.

alternatives.label: Klasies River ESR/TL chronology
alternatives.note: Looser and younger than the single-grain OSL horizon.

entities.summary: A South African tradition of small backed blades, hafted as composite tools, lasting only a few thousand years.

entities.name: Later Stone Age
entities.date_note: Border Cave gives 44.2-43.0 cal BP for the earliest layer. There is no real end date: the Later Stone Age runs on into recorded history, and the value here is a convention for the tree rather than a finding.
entities.summary: The sub-Saharan African tradition of small composite tools that continues into the historical period.

entities.name: Châtelperronian Industry
entities.date_note: In Cantabria it shows no chronological overlap with the local Mousterian, which complicates the usual reading of it as a Neanderthal response to arriving modern humans.
entities.summary: A short-lived western European tradition made during the overlap between Neanderthals and modern humans.

entities.name: Aurignacian Industry
entities.date_note: Arrival dates differ sharply between regional models, from about 43 cal ka BP in southern Iberia to later elsewhere.

alternatives.label: Banks et al. 2013 phase model
alternatives.note: Proto-Aurignacian 41.5-39.9 k cal BP, Early Aurignacian 39.8-37.9 k cal BP.

entities.summary: The first widespread modern-human tradition in Europe, associated with the earliest cave art and figurines.

entities.name: Gravettian Industry
entities.date_note: Bayesian boundaries from the Adriatic basin; regional models differ.
entities.summary: The tradition of the Venus figurines and mammoth-bone dwellings, spanning Europe through the coldest part of the Ice Age.

entities.name: Solutrean Industry
entities.date_note: Bayesian analysis does not confirm the traditional ordering of the internal phases, so the sub-sequence is less secure than the overall span.
entities.summary: An Iberian and French tradition known for slender, finely pressure-flaked laurel-leaf points.

entities.name: Magdalenian Industry
entities.date_note: Preceded by the Badegoulian at 23,092-20,792 cal BP. Regional phase models disagree on the internal sequence.
entities.summary: The late Ice Age tradition of Lascaux and Altamira, ending as the glaciers retreated.

entities.name: Göbekli Tepe
entities.date_note: Only 11 radiocarbon dates exist. The Layer III/II/I scheme has been abandoned for at least eight phases, so phase labels in older sources do not map cleanly.
entities.summary: Monumental enclosures raised by people who were not yet farming, in southeastern Anatolia.

entities.name: Monte Verde II
entities.date_note: Under active challenge: a March 2026 reanalysis proposed a Holocene age, roughly thirty specialists rebutted it in May, and the authors replied in June.

alternatives.label: Surovell et al. 2026
alternatives.note: Argues the dated material is intrusive and the occupation is mid-Holocene.

entities.summary: A settlement in southern Chile whose age broke the Clovis-first model of the peopling of the Americas.

entities.name: Behavioural Firsts
entities.summary: The earliest known evidence for each human behaviour — toolmaking, fire, pigment, burial, art, seafaring. Each date is a floor, not an estimate.
entities.date_note: Starts with the contested Dikika cut marks at 3.39 Ma, which is older than the app's 3.3 Ma floor because the floor tracks the oldest ACCEPTED behaviour and Dikika is not accepted.

entities.name: Stone Knapping
entities.date_note: THE SCOPE FLOOR, defined as a behaviour rather than as a site. Lomekwi 3 is the present evidence, not the definition: the artefacts lie above the Toroto Tuff at 3.31 +/- 0.02 Ma, within the Mammoth reverse subchron. If an older knapping site is accepted, this date moves and the app's scope does not change. Predates the oldest Homo fossil by about 500,000 years, which is why the floor is behavioural and not taxonomic.

alternatives.label: Assemblage not in primary context
alternatives.note: Argues the stratigraphic association with the dated tuff is not established. Offers no alternative date; the implied age is essentially the same. The excavators replied in 2019.

caveats.text: A minority reads the flakes as naturally fractured stone rather than deliberate knapping.

entities.summary: The first deliberate shaping of stone into tools — the behaviour this app uses to mark where human prehistory begins.

entities.name: Butchery of Animals
entities.date_note: The secure record begins 2.6-2.5 Ma at Gona and Bouri, Ethiopia. A claim for 3.39 Ma at Dikika is the older candidate and is not accepted.

alternatives.label: Dikika cut marks
alternatives.note: Marks on two bones claimed as butchery before 3.39 Ma. Critics read them as trampling: 96% of experimental trampling grooves are broad and open, against 4% of genuine cut marks.

caveats.text: The 3.39 Ma Dikika claim is widely read as trampling damage rather than butchery.

entities.summary: Cutting meat from bone with stone tools, which opened a food source that had been out of reach.

entities.name: Controlled Use of Fire
entities.date_note: Wonderwerk Cave Stratum 10 is the standard secure minimum, bracketed by cosmogenic burial ages of 1.27 +/- 0.19 and 0.98 +/- 0.19 Ma. Older claims exist and the field has not settled.

alternatives.label: Wonderwerk Stratum 11
alternatives.note: A 2026 reanalysis pushes burning at the same cave back to 1.79-1.07 Ma.

alternatives.label: Gesher Benot Ya'aqov
alternatives.note: The best-evidenced repeated hearth use, fixed by the Matuyama-Brunhes reversal at 0.79 Ma. Younger than Wonderwerk but less contested.

entities.summary: Keeping and using fire on purpose, which changed diet, safety and how far north people could live.

entities.name: Cooking of Food
entities.date_note: Gesher Benot Ya'aqov, from eight sequential horizons correlated to marine isotope stages 18-20. Note the long gap between the earliest fire and the earliest cooking: the two are not the same behaviour.
entities.summary: Applying controlled heat to food, evidenced by fish teeth heated to a temperature that implies cooking rather than burning.

entities.name: Use of Pigment
entities.date_note: Secure from about 300 ka in both Africa and Europe. Between 1.5 Ma and 300 ka the evidence is sparse and equivocal. Kapthurin GnJh-15 in Kenya is the earliest well-dated assemblage at 0.284 +/- 0.012 Ma.

alternatives.label: Olorgesailie worked pigment
alternatives.note: Described as the oldest clearly worked pigment.

entities.summary: Collecting and working coloured earth, the earliest hint of decoration or marking.

entities.name: Deliberate Burial
entities.date_note: Sima de los Huesos in Spain holds over 7,000 bones from at least 29 individuals, a minimum age since the dated speleothem formed directly on the deposit. Whether accumulation counts as burial is the argument. Qafzeh in Israel at 90-100 ka is the earliest undisputed grave.

alternatives.label: Qafzeh, earliest undisputed grave
alternatives.note: A modern-human burial with fallow-deer antlers placed on the chest, cut into bedrock. Thermoluminescence on burnt flint.

alternatives.label: Homo naledi burial claim
alternatives.note: A 2023 claim of deliberate burial by a small-brained hominin at Rising Star, formally rebutted and not accepted.

caveats.text: Whether the Sima accumulation is burial or another process is unresolved; the Homo naledi claim is rejected by most reviewers.

entities.summary: Placing the dead somewhere on purpose rather than leaving them where they fell.

entities.name: Personal Ornaments
entities.date_note: Bizmoune Cave, Morocco: 33 pierced Tritia gibbosula shells, dated by uranium-series on a speleothem to 142,290 +29,300/-22,060 years at 2 sigma. Explicitly a minimum. Single-grain OSL on the same layer gives ages as young as 57,800 +/- 7,200, which is unresolved.

alternatives.label: Bizmoune OSL chronology
alternatives.note: Optically stimulated luminescence on layer 4c returns a far younger age than the uranium-series speleothem date.

entities.summary: Shells pierced and strung to be worn, which means signalling something about yourself to other people.

entities.name: Abstract Engraving
entities.date_note: Blombos Cave, South Africa: 77 +/- 6 ka by thermoluminescence on burnt lithics for the engraved ochre, with a drawn cross-hatch in ochre crayon at about 73 ka from the same site.

alternatives.label: Trinil engraved shell
alternatives.note: A zigzag engraved on a freshwater mussel shell from Java, attributed to Homo erectus. If accepted it moves this threshold back by 350,000 years.

entities.summary: Deliberate cross-hatched patterns cut into ochre — marks that mean something without depicting anything.

entities.name: Intentional Seafaring
entities.date_note: The colonisation of Sahul recorded at Madjedbebe, Australia: 65 +/- 6 ka at 95.4% by single-grain OSL with Bayesian modelling. Reaching Australia required repeated open-water crossings, so the site dates the voyage as well as the landfall.

alternatives.label: Sceptical reading of the Madjedbebe chronology
alternatives.note: Critics read the same OSL data as about 53 +/- 4 ka, arguing artefacts moved down through the sand.

entities.summary: Crossing open water on purpose, out of sight of the far shore, which requires planning and a built craft.

entities.name: Figurative Art
entities.date_note: A narrative scene at Leang Karampuang, Sulawesi: a warty pig with human figures, dated by laser-ablation uranium-series on the overlying carbonate. A minimum, since the art is older than the crust that formed on it. The 2024 laser-ablation method also pushed the neighbouring Leang Bulu' Sipong 4 scene from 44 ka to about 48 ka.

alternatives.label: European Upper Palaeolithic art
alternatives.note: Chauvet's first occupation is 37,000-33,500 cal BP and the Hohle Fels ivory figurine at least 35,000 years old. Long taken as the earliest figurative art until the Sulawesi dates.

caveats.text: Often said to begin in Ice Age Europe. The oldest known figurative art is in Indonesia and predates Chauvet by some 14,000 years.

entities.summary: Pictures of recognisable things — animals and people — rather than patterns.

entities.name: Lomekwian Industry
entities.date_note: Named from Lomekwi 3. Kept separate from the Oldowan because the knapping technique differs, which is also why the Oldowan's 2.6 Ma start is a definitional boundary rather than the start of toolmaking.
entities.summary: The oldest known stone toolkit: large, heavy cores and flakes struck with techniques unlike the later Oldowan.
